message:
fix(update): the liveness check that only tests ever ran, and a sweep blind to what it existed to stop

Four rejections, and the thread through all of them is the same: a seam a
test fills and production does not, and nobody notices because nothing
fails -- the step simply does not happen.

* Liveness had two answers and production had none. An empty
  isStillRunning meant "assume everything left", which is what shipped, so
  the check existed only in tests. It has three answers now; a lookup that
  cannot complete is Unknown, not Exited, because guessing "gone" starts a
  second copy and guessing "there" reports a machine that is down as a
  success. Empty now means the real check. The identity comparison moved to
  its own translation unit so the relaunch test links the real one -- not
  linking it is how the check came to be unwired in the first place.

* Generalised, because finding these one at a time is not a method:
  UpdateEffectsConfig::unwired() names every empty seam and run() refuses
  to do anything while one is empty. The manifest that was never fetched
  and the version that never reached registration were both this shape.

* Ownership is the handle received at creation, not a pid matched to a
  name. Shell-routed launches are claimed only when exactly one process
  running exactly that image appears between the before and after
  snapshots -- ambiguity is left unowned rather than killed on a guess. A
  rollback does not touch a file while anything it started is unaccounted
  for: half a restore is worse than none, and it reads as the rollback's
  fault.

* Health is asked before any commit. An optional image missing used to
  commit on the spot, and "required started" only means CreateProcess
  returned. A client that did not come back plus a host that started and
  died dropped the backups and called it a partial success. The regression
  for it is here, with a counter-control so it cannot pass by rolling back
  every time.

* Commit reads what DeleteFileW returned. It did not, and cleared the list
  regardless, so a backup that survived left no trace and then blocked the
  NEXT update by holding its name. What cannot be deleted is now moved out
  of the way and recorded -- renaming a file nothing can delete is allowed,
  which is the same asymmetry the swap has always relied on.

And the scenario suite's sweep was blind. It opened each process to read
its image path and skipped the ones it could not open, which were exactly
the processes it existed to stop; they were in the snapshot by name the
whole time. Four survived every run holding their own images, so the next
scenario could not write its starting bytes and failed an assertion about
bytes with no process visible to explain it.
